blocks.html: Massachusetts regulates security deposits tightly. A deposit is the tenant’s money, held under specific requirements about where and how it is kept, with interest and accounting obligations attached, and the penalties for getting it wrong are severe. From an accounting point of view the consequence is simple: a security deposit is a liability on your balance sheet and is not rental income when you receive it. Last month’s rent is treated differently again. The legal side of this belongs with an attorney; the bookkeeping side belongs here, and the two have to agree.

blocks.html: The gain is not the difference between what you paid and what you sold for. It is measured against adjusted basis: purchase price, plus capital improvements, plus certain closing costs, minus all the depreciation you were allowed to claim. Depreciation comes back as recapture at its own rate. Suspended passive losses generally free up. A like-kind exchange can defer the gain, but it has strict deadlines that start running at the closing, so it has to be planned before the property goes under agreement rather than after.

The right way is to record the gross sale, the commission as an expense, the tax as a liability or as remitted by the platform, and then reconcile to the deposit.

blocks.html:
• Massachusetts does not simply mirror the federal code. Depreciation is the familiar example — the federal and Massachusetts write-off for the same asset can differ, which means two sets of records for as long as you own it. That divergence is easy to start and expensive to reconstruct later.
  • The surtax on high income is measured on the whole year. Massachusetts applies an additional tax above a threshold that is adjusted annually, and it looks at total income. A single large event — selling a building, a business, or a large block of stock — can push an ordinary year over the line. That is worth modelling before the closing, not after.
  • Sales and meals tax are their own filings. They are not part of the income tax return, they run on their own calendar, and missing them creates penalties that have nothing to do with how profitable the year was.
  • Estimated payments. Once a business throws off income that is not on a W-2, quarterly estimates start to matter federally and to the Commonwealth. Getting the first year right avoids an underpayment penalty on top of a tax bill you were not expecting.
